Abstract
Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) have rapidly emerged as a pivotal 
innovation for future wireless communication systems, offering a low-power, cost-
efficient means of enhancing spectral efficiency, signal coverage, and network 
adaptability. Composed of metasurfaces with controllable elements, RIS can 
manipulate electromagnetic wave behavior in real time, distinguishing them 
from traditional relaying methods and massive multiple-input multiple-output 
(MIMO) architectures. This article provides a comprehensive overview of RIS 
fundamentals, including recent advances in beam training, channel estimation, and 
their applications in terahertz (THz) and millimeter-wave (mmWave) transmission, 
security frameworks, and electromagnetic information theory (EIT). It also evaluates 
how artificial intelligence (AI) enhances RIS configuration, particularly under near-
field conditions and in complex propagation environments. In addition, the survey 
explores Simultaneously Transmitting and Reflecting RIS (STAR-RIS), which extends 
conventional RIS capabilities by enabling full 360-degree coverage. STAR-RIS 
operates in three distinct modes, Mode Switching (MS), Energy Splitting (ES), and 
Time Switching (TS), making it well-suited for dense user deployments and high 
spectral reuse scenarios. The paper further examines the integration of STAR-RIS with 
non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA), focusing on system design, beamforming 
strategies, and performance metrics such as outage probability, ergodic capacity, and 
symbol error rate. Results show that STAR-RIS-assisted NOMA systems offer significant 
advantages over conventional orthogonal multiple access (OMA) schemes in terms 
of efficiency and reliability. Moreover, this review addresses emerging applications 
of STAR-RIS in unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) communications, vehicular (V2X) 
systems, mobile edge computing (MEC), simultaneous wireless information and 
power transfer (SWIPT), over-the-air computation (AirComp), and cooperative rate 
splitting. It highlights cutting-edge optimization techniques, experimental testbeds, 
and architectural innovations that support practical deployment. Despite their

1  Introduction

growing need for enhanced spectral efficiency, energy conservation, and adaptable net­

providing a passive, adjustable, and cost-efficient approach to controlling signal propa­

Despite its promise, implementing RIS comes with several challenges, particularly

2  Channel estimation and beamforming in RIS-aided systems
RIS consist of a two-dimensional metasurface comprising a large array of tuneable ele­
ments that dynamically adjust the phase, amplitude, or polarization of incoming electro­
magnetic (EM) waves [1]. Unlike conventional relay systems, RIS operates without active 
RF chains, offering a cost-effective and energy-efficient approach to extending wireless 
coverage and managing interference [2]. However, active RIS variants incorporate lim­
ited amplification to mitigate path loss, thereby further enhancing their capabilities [3] 
(Fig. 2).
Compared to traditional massive MIMO, RIS presents an alternative framework for 
improving signal propagation without the reliance on additional power-intensive active 
components [4]. The key advantages of RIS include (Table 1):
 	•
Energy efficiency: Passive RIS consumes significantly less power than conventional 
active beamforming architectures [3].
 	•
Cost-effectiveness: RIS deployment does not require extra base stations or active 
transceivers, making it a financially viable solution [1].

Despite these advantages, RIS-assisted communication systems introduce unique chal­
lenges, particularly in efficient channel estimation, real-time reconfiguration, and intel­

Accurate Channel State Information (CSI) is essential to fully exploit the benefits of 
RIS. Unlike traditional MIMO systems, where CSI acquisition is based on direct mea­
surement at transceivers, RIS lacks active reception capabilities, making indirect channel 
estimation necessary [5]. The key challenges include:
 	•
High dimensionality: Large-scale RIS arrays generate an extensive number of channel 
coefficients that must be estimated [4].
 	•
Passive elements: Since RIS cannot perform direct signal processing, estimation 
must be conducted at the base station or user equipment [5].
 	•
Sparse and correlated channels: Near-field propagation effects and environmental 
obstructions complicate the accuracy of the estimation process [7].
To address these challenges, researchers have explored various innovative approaches, 
including statistical CSI modelling [4], AI-assisted channel estimation [6], and hierarchi­
cal beam training techniques [7].

2.1  Traditional and emerging channel estimation techniques
The challenge of accurately obtaining CSI in RIS-assisted systems has led to the devel­
opment of various estimation techniques. Traditional methods, such as Least Squares 
(LS) and Minimum Mean Square Error (MMSE) estimation, have been widely utilized in 
wireless communications. However, these methods present significant drawbacks when 
applied to RIS-based networks due to their computational complexity and high estima­
tion overhead [5]. Emerging approaches aim to mitigate these limitations by employing:
 	•
Two-timescale channel estimation: Reducing estimation overhead by differentiating 
between fast-varying and slow-varying components [5].
 	•
Hierarchical beam training: Enhancing beam alignment in RIS-aided networks 
through multi-stage refinement processes [7].
 	•
Sparse and compressed sensing methods: Leveraging the sparsity of mmWave and 
THz channels to improve estimation accuracy and efficiency [8].
2.2  AI-driven channel estimation and optimization
Deep learning and artificial intelligence have significantly transformed channel estima­
tion by enabling data-driven optimization techniques [6] (Fig. 3). The primary AI-based 
approaches include:
 	•
Neural network-based CSI prediction: Utilizing deep learning models to predict CSI 
from historical data patterns [6].
 	•
Reinforcement learning for adaptive RIS configuration: Applying reinforcement 
learning algorithms to dynamically adjust RIS phase shifts in response to network 
conditions [6].
 	•
Transformer-based estimation models: Using attention mechanisms to capture spatial 
and temporal dependencies in RIS-assisted communication channels, improving 
estimation performance [6].

2.4  Practical implementation and emerging channel estimation techniques
Recent studies have significantly advanced the practical design, prototyping, and estima­
tion strategies for RIS-aided wireless systems. For instance, a 256-element RIS prototype 
integrating both phase shift and radiation functionalities demonstrated 21.7 dBi gain at 
2.3 GHz and 19.1 dBi at 28.5 GHz, highlighting its potential for enhanced power effi­
ciency compared to traditional phased arrays [9].
In the domain of channel estimation, deep learning has been employed to improve 
performance in mmWave massive MIMO. The GM-LAMP algorithm, a Gaussian mix­
ture-based learned approximate message passing method has outperformed conven­
tional iterative techniques in both accuracy and efficiency [10]. Similarly, optimization 
frameworks have been proposed to jointly tune RIS reflection coefficients and hybrid 
precoders at the base station, achieving significant spectral efficiency with low computa­
tional complexity [11].
Double-structured orthogonal matching pursuit (DS-OMP) algorithms have also 
emerged, significantly reducing pilot overhead while maintaining estimation accuracy 
in RIS-aided systems [12, 13]. For wideband THz massive MIMO scenarios, beam split 
effects pose unique challenges. Novel solutions, including enhanced sparse estimation 
and beam zooming techniques, have been introduced to counteract these limitations 
and ensure precise user tracking across broad frequency ranges [14, 15].
RIS integration into cell-free networks has demonstrated notable benefits by replacing 
some base stations with RIS units, thereby reducing power consumption and improving 
network capacity through joint precoding designs [16]. Moreover, two-timescale chan­
nel estimation frameworks have been proposed, where quasi-static and mobile compo­
nents are separated to minimize pilot overhead while preserving CSI fidelity [17].
Efficient feedback mechanisms have also been explored. For example, dimension-
reduced channel feedback schemes leverage channel sparsity to reduce overhead by 
over 80% in RIS-aided FDD systems while maintaining high precision [18]. In mobile 
environments, transformer-based models have been employed for parallel channel pre­
diction, significantly improving adaptability and reducing error propagation through 
attention-based mechanisms [19].

2.5  Near-field challenges and RIS architecture comparisons
As systems evolve toward Extremely Large-Scale Antenna Arrays (ELAA), the limita­
tions of planar-wave models become apparent. Near-field spherical wave modeling is 
crucial for understanding spatial focusing and beamforming accuracy in dense environ­
ments. Studies have emphasized the need for novel estimation and beam training strate­
gies tailored for ELAA systems [20].
Additionally, comparative evaluations of active and passive RIS have revealed critical 
trade-offs. While passive RIS suffer from multiplicative fading, active RIS overcome this 
drawback by incorporating amplification. Experimental results show a 130% increase in 
sum-rate gain with active RIS, compared to just 22% with passive RIS, highlighting the 
superiority of active elements in enhancing spectral efficiency and robustness [21].
3  THz/mmWave communications and electromagnetic information theory
The integration of terahertz (THz) and millimeter-wave (mmWave) frequency bands into 
next-generation wireless networks is pivotal for achieving the ultra-high data rates and 
low latency requirements anticipated in 6G systems. Despite their potential, these high-
frequency bands are inherently challenged by severe path loss, molecular absorption, 
beam misalignment, and the pronounced impact of near-field propagation effects. RIS 
have garnered significant attention as an enabling technology to mitigate these impair­
ments through programmable reflection, dynamic beamforming, and channel reconfigu­
ration. This section provides a comprehensive examination of recent advancements in 
RIS-assisted THz/mmWave communications, with particular focus on near-field beam­
forming strategies, practical deployment considerations, and optimization of RIS phase 
shifts. Moreover, the application of EIT is discussed as a rigorous analytical framework 
to enhance capacity modeling and facilitate the efficient design of RIS-enabled high-fre­
quency wireless systems.
3.1  THz band communication for next-generation networks
THz communication provides ultra-high data rates and vast spectrum availabil­
ity, making it a key enabler for next-generation networks. However, its adoption faces 
considerable challenges, including severe path loss, molecular absorption, and beam 
misalignment. RIS have been proposed as a solution to mitigate these limitations by 
dynamically optimizing reflection and beamforming strategies [8].
3.2  Near-field effects and beam split challenges
With the transition to THz and mmWave frequencies, near-field propagation effects 
become more pronounced, leading to challenges such as beam split and wavefront cur­
vature distortions. To address these issues, emerging solutions such as dynamic RIS-
assisted beamforming and hybrid precoding techniques have been developed [7].
3.3  Practical implementation and future directions
Experimental studies have validated the feasibility of THz RIS-assisted communication; 
however, scalability and energy efficiency remain key concerns. Future research should 
focus on designing low-power RIS architectures and enhancing integration with existing 
cellular networks for practical deployment [8].

THz communication offers ultra-high data rates but suffers from high path loss and 
molecular absorption. RIS has been investigated as a means to counteract these chal­

3.5  THz precoding for 6G networks
THz communication delivers ultra-wide bandwidth but is prone to high path loss and 
beam misalignment. The study in [23] explores key THz precoding methods, includ­
ing analogue beamforming, hybrid precoding, and RIS-based precoding. Their research 
demonstrates that incorporating RIS into THz precoding strategies significantly 
enhances energy efficiency and spectral utilization, making it a promising technique for 
6G networks.
3.6  Fundamentals of electromagnetic information theory (EIT)
EIT provides a comprehensive theoretical framework for analysing and optimizing wire­
less communication in environments influenced by electromagnetic fields [22]. Unlike 
traditional information theory, EIT accounts for wave propagation, field distributions, 
and scattering effects, making it a crucial tool for enhancing the performance of RIS-
assisted systems. By incorporating electromagnetic field principles, EIT enables more 
accurate modelling of wireless channels and improves the efficiency of RIS-based signal 
processing.
3.7  Capacity limits in RIS-aided systems
Recent studies have investigated the capacity limits of RIS-assisted wireless networks 
across different configurations. Research findings suggest that integrating RIS with 
large-scale MIMO architectures can significantly enhance spectral efficiency while 
reducing overall power consumption [4]. Theoretical models have been developed to 
quantify the capacity improvements achieved through RIS-assisted beamforming and 
intelligent reflection control, demonstrating substantial gains in system throughput and 
energy efficiency.
3.8  Optimization of RIS phase shifts for capacity maximization
One of the fundamental challenges in RIS deployment is the optimization of phase shifts 
to maximize network capacity. Various strategies have been proposed to dynamically 
adjust RIS configurations in real time, including:
 	•
Convex optimization: Formulating phase shift control as an optimization problem to 
achieve the best signal enhancement.
 	•
Deep reinforcement learning (DRL): Leveraging AI-based techniques to adaptively 
tune RIS phase shifts based on real-time channel conditions [6].
 	•
Heuristic algorithms: Applying rule-based and evolutionary approaches to efficiently 
configure RIS elements for enhanced capacity.

3.9  Impact of near-field effects on capacity enhancement
Near-field propagation effects introduce unique challenges in RIS-assisted systems,

4  Security, interference mitigation, and deployment challenges
As RIS become increasingly integral to next-generation wireless networks, ensuring their 
secure and reliable deployment emerges as a paramount concern. While RIS technology 
offers promising enhancements in signal control, spectral efficiency, and interference 
management, it simultaneously introduces unique vulnerabilities due to its passive and 
programmable nature. These include susceptibility to signal manipulation, eavesdrop­
ping, and jamming—threats not traditionally encountered in conventional communica­
tion architectures. Moreover, interference mitigation and practical deployment of RIS in 
dense, dynamic environments pose additional technical challenges. This section pres­
ents a detailed exploration of the evolving security landscape for RIS-assisted systems, 
encompassing physical layer security (PLS) techniques, interference suppression strate­
gies, and mutual information frameworks grounded in EIT. Furthermore, it highlights 
emerging research directions, including AI-based intrusion detection, hardware-aware 
security designs, and robust deployment models aimed at realizing scalable and secure 
RIS integration for 6G wireless communication.
4.1  Security challenges in RIS-enabled networks
With the increasing adoption of RIS technology, security concerns as shown in Fig. 4, 
such as signal manipulation, eavesdropping, and jamming attacks have become critical 
[24]. Unlike traditional communication systems, RIS-assisted networks introduce novel 
vulnerabilities due to the passive nature of RIS elements, which can be exploited for 
unauthorized data interception.
4.2  RIS for physical layer security
To enhance security in RIS-assisted networks, physical layer security (PLS) techniques 
have been proposed. These strategies include:
 	•
Artificial noise (AN) injection: Introducing artificial noise to confuse potential 
eavesdroppers as shown in Fig. 4 [24].
 	•
Secure beamforming: Adjusting RIS reflection patterns to maximize secrecy rates 
[24].
 	•
Secrecy rate maximization: Optimizing RIS phase shifts to minimize information 
leakage.

5  AI-driven optimization and learning-based RIS control
The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface 
(RIS)-assisted wireless communication systems marks a transformative shift in how 
adaptive and intelligent radio environments are realized. As RIS networks scale in com­
plexity and operate under dynamic, non-stationary conditions, conventional optimiza­
tion and estimation techniques fall short of delivering real-time, high-accuracy control. 
AI-driven methodologies, particularly those leveraging deep learning, reinforcement 
learning, and transformer-based models, have emerged as powerful tools to enhance 
channel estimation, beamforming, and system-level optimization. This section explores 
recent advancements in AI-enabled RIS control, including mobility-aware channel pre­
diction, federated learning for decentralized inference, and hybrid-field estimation for 
extremely large-scale MIMO (XL-MIMO) systems. Moreover, the discussion extends to 
novel architectures such as user-specific RIS, active sub-connected configurations, and 
end-to-end learning frameworks, all of which contribute to improved spectral efficiency, 
fairness, and scalability in next-generation wireless networks.

10.5  Emerging applications beyond communication

Beyond theoretical modeling and high-level system design, the practical implemen­
tation of RIS and STAR-RIS requires careful attention to physical-layer considerations 
such as material selection, metasurface architecture, and inter-element electromagnetic 
interactions. Recent studies have highlighted the significant impact of hardware impair­
ments, including phase noise, finite-resolution phase shifters, and amplifier non-linear­
ities, on the achievable performance of RIS-assisted mmWave systems. For example, 
Gong et al. [80] investigate beamforming design under such hardware limitations and 
reveal how impairments lead to mean square error floors and rate saturation in high-
SNR regimes. Furthermore, RIS structures with sub-wavelength inter-element spacing 
are subject to mutual coupling effects, which create non-diagonal scattering behaviors 
and challenge the assumptions of ideal phase control. In [81], an electromagnetically 
consistent model is proposed that optimizes scattering parameters using S-parame­
ters, significantly improving system performance by capturing realistic coupling inter­
actions. Additionally, foundational works such as [82] offer a comprehensive overview 
of RIS hardware architecture, control strategies, and reflective surface materials, rein­
forcing the importance of scalable and power-efficient physical implementations. These 
perspectives underline the necessity of hardware-aware modeling and experimental vali­
dation to ensure that theoretical gains can translate into robust real-world deployments.

11  Emerging trends and extensions in intelligent metasurfaces
In addition to the foundational and widely adopted developments in RIS and STAR-RIS, 
several recent works have proposed innovative extensions that push the boundaries of 
metasurface-assisted wireless communications. These emerging directions encompass 
stacked metasurface architectures, flexible intelligent surfaces, advanced channel pre­
diction techniques, and transceiver-agnostic configurations. A summary of these contri­
butions is presented in Table 7, with key themes briefly discussed below.
11.1  Stacked intelligent metasurfaces
Stacked or multilayer metasurfaces have been introduced to overcome limitations of 
single-layer RIS, particularly for applications in holographic MIMO systems and direc­
tion-of-arrival (DoA) estimation. These works propose integrating multiple metasurface 
layers to enable enhanced spatial resolution, polarization diversity, and improved angu­
lar coverage. For instance, the use of stacked metasurfaces for 2D DoA estimation dem­
onstrates significant gains in angular resolution without increasing surface area.
11.2  Low-complexity beamforming and codebook approaches
To reduce training overhead and computational load, codebook-based passive beam­
forming (PBF) and channel estimation (CE) schemes have emerged. These methods 
pre-define a limited set of beam patterns or transformation matrices, enabling faster 
adaptation in practical deployments. Such solutions are critical for scenarios involv­
ing quantized phase shifts or massive RIS deployments where overhead becomes a 
bottleneck.

11.3  Predictive and learning-based channel modeling
Deep learning is increasingly being applied to RIS-assisted systems, especially for time-
varying channels. One notable contribution proposes a neural network-based CSI pre­
dictor that captures the dynamics of MU-MISO networks under RIS support. These 
models reduce reliance on instantaneous CSI and offer generalization across mobility 
patterns and fading conditions.
11.4  Flexible and transceiver-agnostic architectures
Beyond conventional RIS, flexible and programmable metasurfaces are being developed 
to support dynamically adaptable reflection/transmission behaviors. Simultaneously, 
hardware design strategies that decouple RIS configuration from specific transceiver 
characteristics (e.g., antenna selection) are gaining traction, promoting broader interop­
erability and modularity in real-world systems.
Collectively, these emerging approaches extend the current RIS/STAR-RIS paradigm 
and open up new directions for future research, particularly in energy-aware design, 
real-time adaptation, and 6G-oriented metasurface deployments. These papers also 
highlight gaps in existing benchmarking methods and hardware scalability that warrant 
further exploration.
12  Conclusion
RIS represent a paradigm shift in wireless communication, offering unprecedented con­
trol over electromagnetic wave propagation. This paper has provided a comprehensive 
review of fundamental concepts, key advancements, and future research directions in 
RIS technology.
As the wireless industry moves toward 6G and beyond, continued innovation in AI-
driven optimization, security enhancements, and scalable hardware solutions will be 
essential for realizing the full potential of RIS. The integration of RIS into next-gener­
ation networks is expected to revolutionize wireless communications, enabling intelli­
gent, energy-efficient, and high-capacity connectivity across various applications.
STAR-RIS technology marks a significant advancement in reconfigurable intelligent 
surfaces, providing full-space coverage and enhanced signal control. When combined 
with NOMA, STAR-RIS improves spectral efficiency, sum rate, and fairness in multi-
user scenarios. The reviewed studies highlight its potential for 6G networks, demon­
strating key advantages over conventional RIS. However, optimization challenges and 
hardware limitations remain, requiring further research before large-scale real-world 
deployment.

tions, beamforming optimization, and multi-RIS cooperation strategies, paving the way

While RIS have shown great potential, several key challenges must be overcome to 
facilitate their seamless integration into next-generation wireless networks. Future 
research should focus on the following areas:
 	•
AI-driven RIS optimization: The application of deep reinforcement learning, federated 
learning, and transformer-based models can enhance the real-time adaptation of RIS 
phase shifts, optimizing energy efficiency and network performance.
 	•
Scalable and cost-effective RIS hardware: Developing low-cost, scalable RIS 
architectures with improved power efficiency is crucial for widespread deployment, 
particularly in dense urban and IoT-based networks.
 	•
Standardization 
and 
interoperability: 
Establishing 
global 
standards 
and 
interoperability frameworks for RIS deployment will ensure seamless integration 
with existing 5G and future 6G networks.
 	•
Security and interference mitigation: Implementing advanced security mechanisms, 
such as AI-driven intrusion detection, secure beamforming, and physical layer 
security, will be essential to address emerging threats in RIS-aided networks.
 	•
Near-field propagation and THz/mmWave communications: Further exploration of 
near-field effects, hybrid precoding techniques, and dynamic beam training will be 
necessary to maximize RIS performance in high-frequency communication bands.
 	•
Experimental validation and large-scale deployments: Bridging the gap between 
theoretical models and real-world implementations through testbeds and large-scale 
experimental deployments will be crucial for advancing RIS technology.
While STAR-RIS-assisted NOMA networks show promising theoretical and experimen­
tal results, several challenges remain:
 	•
Channel estimation complexity: The need for accurate CSI increases system 
overhead, necessitating low-complexity estimation techniques.
 	•
Hardware limitations: The practical implementation of STAR-RIS with independent 
transmission and reflection control is still in its early stages, requiring further 
advancements in hardware design.
 	•
Energy efficiency: While active STAR-RIS elements enhance performance, they also 
consume additional power, necessitating efficient power allocation strategies.
 	•
Security concerns: The full-space signal propagation enabled by STAR-RIS introduces 
new security vulnerabilities, requiring robust physical layer security mechanisms to 
prevent eavesdropping and attacks.
Potential future research directions include:
 	•
Hybrid STAR-RIS architectures: Combining passive and active elements to balance 
energy efficiency and performance.
 	•
Deep learning-based CSI prediction: Leveraging AI models for real-time adaptive 
beamforming.
 	•
Joint optimization of STAR-RIS and AI-driven resource allocation: Enhancing large-
scale NOMA networks through AI-based decision-making.

While STAR-RIS-assisted NOMA networks demonstrate strong theoretical and experi­
mental potential, their practical deployment involves key trade-offs that must be care­
fully addressed. Enhanced spectral efficiency and full-space coverage come at the cost 
of increased hardware complexity, energy consumption, and channel estimation over­
head. The flexibility of transmission and reflection control introduces new challenges in 
secure beamforming and real-time optimization. Therefore, future research should focus 
on developing hybrid active–passive STAR-RIS architectures, efficient power allocation 
strategies, and robust AI-driven CSI prediction methods to balance performance with 
complexity. Addressing these trade-offs will be essential for enabling scalable, secure, 
and energy-efficient STAR-RIS integration in next-generation wireless systems.

Abstract: Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) have rapidly emerged as a pivotal innovation for future wireless communication systems, offering a low-power, cost- efficient means of enhancing spectral efficiency, signal coverage, and network adaptability. Composed of metasurfaces with controllable elements, RIS can manipulate electromagnetic wave behavior in real time, distinguishing them from traditional relaying methods and massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) architectures. This article provides a comprehensive overview of RIS fundamentals, including recent advances in beam training, channel estimation, and their applications in terahertz (THz) and millimeter-wave (mmWave) transmission, security frameworks, and electromagnetic information theory (EIT). It also evaluates how artificial intelligence (AI) enhances RIS configuration, particularly under near- field conditions and in complex propagation environments. In addition, the survey explores Simultaneously Transmitting and Reflecting RIS (STAR-RIS), which extends conventional RIS capabilities by enabling full 360-degree coverage. STAR-RIS operates in three distinct modes, Mode Switching (MS), Energy Splitting (ES), and Time Switching (TS), making it well-suited for dense user deployments and high spectral reuse scenarios. The paper further examines the integration of STAR-RIS with non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA), focusing on system design, beamforming strategies, and performance metrics such as outage probability, ergodic capacity, and symbol error rate. Results show that STAR-RIS-assisted NOMA systems offer significant advantages over conventional orthogonal multiple access (OMA) schemes in terms of efficiency and reliability. Moreover, this review addresses emerging applications of STAR-RIS in unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) communications, vehicular (V2X) systems, mobile edge computing (MEC), simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (SWIPT), over-the-air computation (AirComp), and cooperative rate splitting. It highlights cutting-edge optimization techniques, experimental testbeds, and architectural innovations that support practical deployment. Despite their considerable potential, RIS and STAR-RIS face key challenges, including complex channel state information (CSI) acquisition, hardware scalability, adaptation to dynamic environments, and security risks.
